194	Everything else on the wire is **refused before translation**, by an allowlist, not a denylist: `env.resolve` returns secret values; the `env.*` writes, `definition.install`, `project.add`, `project.root`, `set.sync`, `workflow.*`, `dispatch.runner`, `session.kill` and `session.remove` change what runs on the host or what it keeps. v1 remote is the table above and nothing more.
195	
196	**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
197	  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
198	  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
199	  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
200	  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
201	  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
202	  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in design.md's trust boundary is widened to "or as redacted text on the remote port".
203	
204	New read models, added to the wire crate:
205	
206	- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
207	- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
208	- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
209	- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
210	  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
211	  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
212	  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
213	  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
214	  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
215	  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
216	  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
217	- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.

221	### 4.4 WebSocket events
222	
223	Envelope:
224	
225	```json
226	{
227	  "server_id": "uuid",
228	  "epoch": "uuid",
229	  "revision": 1042,
230	  "type": "changed",
231	  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
232	  "at_ms": 1760220000000
233	}
234	```
235	
236	Event types:
237	
238	- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
239	- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
240	- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
241	- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
242	- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
243	- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.
244	
245	**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:
246	
247	1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
248	2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
249	   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
250	   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
251	   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
252	   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
253	   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
254	3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.
255	
256	**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.
257	
258	**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.
259	
260	**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:
261	
262	1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
263	2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
264	3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
265	4. enables commands.
266	
267	Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.

269	### 4.5 Commands
270	
271	- `send`, `resume` and `trust` are authenticated actions under `control` scope against one owning server and session.
272	- The client makes a UUID operation id per command and sends it as the wire `op`.
273	- **Logged before run.** Today `operations.log` gets a request line only for creations, and the reply line after the command ran; `serve` skips a command only when a reply line exists. That leaves a crash between sending keys and appending the reply as a repeat on retry. The port closes that gap for every non-replayable command (`Class::NonReplayable`: `session.send`, `session.resume`): `serve` appends the request line **before** dispatch, and a failed append refuses the command without running it. On arrival, an op with a request line and no reply line is answered `interrupted` and **not run again**; an op with a reply line is answered from it. `session.trust` is `Idempotent` on the wire and needs neither.
274	- The client's rule per `/ops/{op}` status:
275	  - `done`: use the reply;
276	  - `interrupted`: the host started it and the outcome is unknown; never resubmit; show the session's current state and let the user decide;
277	  - `unknown`: the host never received it (nothing was logged, and the frame answers queued requests in arrival order, so a request that had reached the frame before the status query has a line); resubmitting with the same op is safe.
278	  A timeout on a command is followed by a status query, never by a blind resend.
279	- `send` puts keys into the pane, as the app's own message box does. "Accepted" means the keys were sent. Progress is the record's state: `PromptSubmitted`, then working, then `Stop` with the new last response. A send to a pane sitting at Claude Code's folder trust question is accepted but goes nowhere until `trust` answers it; the session view carries `trust_question`, and the client shows the same "Trust this folder" button the app shows.
280	- `resume` on a not-running agent is user-initiated, so allowed, but the client confirms it ("Resume spends a turn") before sending; the host never resumes on its own.
281	- Failures name the reason: not running, not resumable, unknown record, scope missing, pairing revoked, log unavailable.
282	- **A new session (2026-10-19).** `POST projects/{id}/sessions` under `control` opens a session in the project, through the same `session.new` the CLI and Dispatch use, with the body's `op` as the key: `{op, name, kind, cwd, prompt}`, `kind` one of `claude`, `codex` or `shell` (a command or a service is not opened from a device), `cwd` the project's root when absent and otherwise a directory under it, relative or absolute, refused `bad_request` when it steps out of the root or is not a directory, so a device never opens a shell elsewhere on the disk; `prompt` is an agent's first message, on its command line as the CLI puts it, so the agent is already working when the device opens the window. The reply is the command body with `made: [{kind: "session", id}]`; `/ops/{op}` carries `made` too, so a creation whose reply was lost still names its record. `info` lists `create`. The client offers it on a host that is connected, paired under `control` and serves `create`: a plus button on the Sessions tab and "New session in this project" on a listed session, opening a sheet with the host, the project by workspace, the kind, a name (the kind's word and a count when none is typed), a directory and the first message; Start posts it, reads the project's sessions again and opens the new session's window.
283	
284	**The draft.** An agent session's prompt on the host is its Prompt Box editor (design.md, "Prompt Box status"), one document with undo, the live utterance as a provisional span, voice commands and the AI pass. A device does not keep a prompt of its own: it reads the editor's draft and works on it, so dictation from the headset, dictation at the desk and typing on either meet in one text, and a prompt begun on one device can be finished on the other. The editor exists whether or not the session is drawn on the host, as it does for a card's microphone.
285	
286	- `GET sessions/{id}/draft` (any paired device) answers `{draft: {text, live, status, status_text, can_undo, can_redo, ai, busy}}`: the rendered text, the byte range of the utterance still being recognized or null, the editor's status (`idle`, `listening`, `finishing`, `degraded`, `error`) with its reason, whether undo and redo apply, whether the host has an `OpenAI` key for the AI pass, and whether a pass is running. Only an agent session has a draft (`no_draft` otherwise). The host emits `changed {draft, id}` for an editor whose draft moved, fingerprinted a few times a second while a subscriber is connected, and a device holding the draft re-reads it; no watch is needed, since the editor is the host's own state rather than a source the worker polls.
287	- `POST sessions/{id}/draft` (control) applies one of the editor's tools and answers with the draft as it stands: `{action: "replace", text}` sets the text whole (what the device typed; last writer wins, one person), `undo`, `redo`, `clear`, `clean_up` (the AI pass, refused `failed` when the host has no key), `delete_sentence`, `delete_paragraph`, and `{action: "send", op}`, which takes the draft's text to the pane exactly as `session.send` does, under the device's op as the key, and clears the editor when it went; a repeat of a send that went is answered from the log. A send of an empty draft is refused.
288	- `POST sessions/{id}/dictation` (control) carries `{session, events}`: the device's recognizer session, a number the device picks apart from the host's own, and its speech events in order, each `{sequence, kind, utterance, revision, text}` with `kind` one of `started`, `voice_started`, `partial`, `final`, `voice_ended`, `stopped`. The host feeds them to the editor as its own recognizer's events: `started` puts the editor's status at listening, a partial is the provisional span revised in place, a final commits the utterance at its anchor, `stopped` returns the status to idle. At most 256 events of 16 KiB each per request. The reply is the draft as it stands, so the device sees its words land without waiting for the event. The device segments speech into utterances itself (the Apple recognizer starts over after a pause and closes an utterance by re-sending its words later); the editor keeps the document. Two recognizers into one editor (the desk's and the headset's) are kept apart by their session numbers.
289	
290	### 4.6 Dispatch and waiting
291	
292	"Waiting on you" on a card includes reasons set from outside: Dispatch marks a session through `session.waiting` when one of its tickets needs a decision. `SessionView.waiting_reason` is already on the wire; the client shows it. The `Dispatch · <project>` working sets are ordinary sets to the client.
293	
294	#### 4.7 Tickets
295	
296	The ticket view on a device (2026-10-17) reads Dispatch through the Switchboard port, not Dispatch's own socket, which only the Mac reaches: the port serves what the app already holds from its two-second status poll, so a device costs the runner nothing. `GET dispatch/tickets` is the core's `TicketListing` (`src/core/tickets.rs`): `connected` (a runner answered the last poll; without one the tickets are the last seen), the `projects` with a pipeline (slots, running, pending, waiting on me, the queue, the supervisor's session id), and the `tickets` by project then oldest first, never the runner's write order. Each ticket is a summary: source, state and reason, the current stage's name among the `stages`, `standing` worded exactly as the Mac's page words it (`1 waiting on you`, `plan running`, `parked: <reason>`, `held: <why>`), `waits` and `urgent` as the page colours it, `current_session` and `root_project`, and every decision with its question, options, recommendation, `multiple`, state, answer and `needs_note`. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}` adds the body (bounded at the notes cap), the attempts with the session each ran in and the pull request it is bound to, the lanes by branch, and the holds; paths stay on the Mac. The collection is one resource, `tickets` with an empty id, fingerprinted with everything else: a decision made or answered, a stage moved, or the runner coming or going is one `changed` frame, to every subscriber.
297	
298	Two commands under `control`, each the Mac's own action and so Dispatch's own call: `decide` takes `{decision, answer, note?}` (the decision's id; for a `multiple` decision the options joined by commas) and is checked against the last status before anything runs (the decision pending, every option among the decision's, a note where the option needs one), and `resume` a parked ticket. The reply is deferred until Dispatch answers the call, through the same channel the content worker answers on: `{decision}` or `{ticket}` on success, the runner's reason as `failed` or `not_found`, `dispatch_off` (503) when no runner answers. A decision already answered as asked is answered again from the record, so a device that lost the reply repeats at no cost; one answered otherwise is `answered` (409). `info` lists `tickets` among the capabilities, and a client treats a host without it as having no tickets.
299	
300	The files of each attempt (2026-10-18) ride on the single-ticket read: `TicketAttempt.files` names each artifact the attempt wrote (its notes, a plan, a review summary), the log of the stage's checks, each review round's findings and response, and every file of its evidence directory, with a `kind`, whether it is `inline` text or an `image`, and for evidence its size and time. A file is named by a `key`, a hash of its path, so the path stays on the Mac; a secret artifact is listed as `secret` and never read. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` answers `{key, text}` for text, through the Mac's own `DispatchReadArtifact` (so Dispatch's refusals, of a secret or of a file outside the ticket, are the device's answer, and a text the Mac already holds for the ticket as it stands is answered from its cache), bounded at 256 KiB; for an evidence image it answers `{key, media, data}` with the bytes as base64, read from the disk here, up to 700 KiB (`too_large`, 413, beyond that). `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` is the ticket's event log as the Mac's cache holds it after its `DispatchReadEvents`, `{events, last, unavailable}`, served from the cache while the ticket has not changed; both reads are deferred until Dispatch answers, as the commands are. `close` is the third command, refused as `not_closable` (409) unless the status says the ticket may be closed. The attempt also carries its `checks` (head and exit) and its review `rounds`. `info` lists `evidence` for all of this, and a client shows a host without it the files by name only.
301	
302	## 5. Security and pairing
303	
304	A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.
305	
306	- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
307	- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
308	- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
309	- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
310	- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
311	- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
312	- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
313	- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
314	- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
315	- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
316	- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.
317	- The client verifies the pin on every connection and on endpoint changes; a mismatch is shown as "identity changed, pair again" and never auto-merged.
318	- Validate input, cap request bodies at 64 KiB, cap `lines` on `screen` (the wire clamps to 200) and `run_output` (500), cap pages and bodies as §4.2 says, and keep tokens out of logs, URLs, Bonjour TXT records and crash reports. Refusals are logged by op and kind, never with content.
319	- Loopback-only without auth is acceptable **only inside the spike directory**. No milestone commit binds a non-loopback interface without pairing.
320	
321	## 6. Discovery and connection lifecycle
322	
323	### 6.1 Discovery
324	
325	- The host advertises `_switchboard._tcp` while listening on a LAN interface.
326	- The Apple client browses with `Network.framework`.
327	- `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` and `NSBonjourServices` (`_switchboard._tcp`) in the Apple app manifests.
328	- Manual host and port entry for networks where mDNS is blocked.
329	- Known servers and pinned identities are persisted separately from transient discovery results.
330	- A changed IP address is not a new server.
331	- A host that is not connected is resolved again from its Bonjour record before each retry: a host that died sends no goodbye for its old record, so a browse alone does not report the move.
332	- A discovered record whose host is not yet paired offers pairing by the typed code (§5).
333	
334	### 6.2 Per-host state machine
335	
336	`discovered -> unpaired -> pairing -> connecting -> syncing -> connected -> reconnecting/offline`
337	
338	- A failed connection to host A never blocks host B.
339	- Bounded exponential backoff with jitter; reconnect promptly on network changes and on the app returning to the foreground (visionOS and iPadOS drop the socket in the background; cached snapshots cover the gap).
340	- On reconnect: verify the pin, present the token, check `/info` for protocol compatibility and epoch, subscribe, snapshot, reconcile (§4.4), then enable commands.
341	- Errors surface per host.
342	- Unsupported protocol versions are shown explicitly.
343	
344	## 7. Swift client structure
345	
346	Suggested modules:
347	
348	- **SwitchboardProtocol:** Codable models mirroring the wire views, typed requests, version negotiation, the event envelope.
349	- **SwitchboardTransport:** HTTPS/WSS transport with the pinning delegate (`URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` share it), bearer auth, reconnection, discovery.
350	- **SwitchboardClientCore:** `ServerRegistry`, `ConnectionManager`, per-server stores with the event buffer and revision reconciliation, `UnifiedStore`, command routing, cached snapshots with a per-server budget (pages of a conversation evicted furthest from the view first).
351	
352	**What the client keeps, and where.** Persisted, in the app's container: the known-server list (`server_id`, display name, last addresses, enabled flag) and the user's presentation state (workspaces, view instances, window ids, per-view mode and position, server filters). In the Keychain: the bearer token and the pinned key hash per server. **In memory only**: every read model and every content body (session metadata, conversations, last responses, screen text, run output, file content) and any unsent draft. Nothing from a host is written to disk, so there is no data-protection class to choose and no purge schedule; relaunching the client starts from the server list and refetches. Offline, the cached snapshots of §3.2 are what memory holds since the last connection, and they go with the process. Per-server memory budget: 32 MiB of content, evicted furthest from any open view first. **Forget server** removes its token, pin, server entry, memory and every view instance on it; **revocation** or an **identity change** seen on a connection drops the token and the memory at once, marks the server as needing pairing, and keeps the view instances so they can be refilled after a new pairing. A cached body is never shown as current without its connection: every disconnected view says so.
353	- **SwitchboardUI:** shared SwiftUI card, last-response, conversation, run-output, working-set, server selector and connection status views.
354	- **SwitchboardVision:** visionOS entry, spatial `WindowGroup`s, card pop-out lifecycle.
355	- **SwitchboardPad:** iPadOS entry and platform-appropriate multiwindow navigation.
356	
357	One `ServerConnection` actor per known host. The aggregate store exposes qualified references and derived views. UI never builds host URLs to fetch an item.
358	
359	### 7.1 Presentation model
360	
361	Separate:
362	
363	1. **Resource:** a session, working set or pinned file owned by a server.
364	2. **View instance:** a presentation of that resource, with mode (`compact`, `last_response`, `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output`), selection, scroll and disclosure state, and a unique view-instance id. The mode set depends on the session's kind: `conversation` and `last_response` exist for Claude Code sessions, `screen` for every running session, `run_output` for commands and services.
365	3. **Workspace:** a saved collection of view instances and client-side organization. **A workspace is cross-host by construction**: its view instances refer to qualified resources, so one workspace may hold views on any combination of paired servers, with no coordinating server and no host-side resource for it. A host's working sets stay host-owned (§8); a workspace is the client's own grouping over them.
366	
367	The same resource can be shown in several views without duplicating anything. Client-side window and view state is never sent to the host. The per-server store counts the view instances interested in each content key and sends `watch` and `unwatch` only on the transitions between zero and one (§4.4).
368	
369	### 7.2 visionOS windows
370	
371	- Main window: combined browsing with list, grid and focus modes and server filters. Card sizes follow the host's grid rectangles only as a hint; the client lays out for its own space.
372	- Card window group: `WindowGroup(for: CardWindowRequest.self)` keyed by a stable window-instance id and a qualified ref.
373	- `openWindow` and `dismissWindow` create and close windows; the system positions them.
374	- Closing a window never stops a session.
375	- Per-view mode and navigation state survive, keyed by `(resume_id, turn n)` for conversation position.
376	- When a server goes offline, windows stay open on cached content with controls disabled. A `removed` event marks the window and disables its controls; the window stays until the user closes it.
377	
378	### 7.3 iPadOS reuse
379	
380	- Reuse protocol, transport, stores, presentation models and most views.
381	- Adapt multiwindow behavior to iPadOS scenes.
382	- No RealityKit or visionOS-only APIs in shared packages.
383	
384	## 8. Unified browsing and filtering
385	
386	- Default view: all connected hosts, with source labels.
387	- Filter by server, working set, session kind, and state (`CardState` labels: waiting on you, working, idle, starting, exited, not running, not resumable).
388	- Sorting across hosts: the host's own rank (waiting first, then working, starting, idle, exited, not running, mirroring `CardState::rank`), then last activity, then record id as the tie-breaker.
389	- Server management screen: discovered and known servers, status, pairing, rename, enable/disable, forget.
390	- Working sets with the same name on different servers stay separate by qualified id; the UI groups by source.
391	- No client-made cross-host working set in v1. The host's sets are read-only from the client.
392	
393	## 9. Remote access later
394	
395	Every server is an authenticated endpoint; nothing assumes RFC1918 addresses or Bonjour. A future Tailscale or WireGuard route, a manual remote endpoint, or an outbound relay reuses the same protocol, token and pinned key. No relay in v1. The pin is bound to the installation's key, not to an address or a certificate's validity window, so a route change or a reissued certificate does not invalidate it.

exec` sends it with `env.resolve`; the record keeps only its SHA-256.
  To try `switchboard-env` by hand, run it in a shell the app launched,
  after `env-setup unlock` (or the settings menu's Unlock environment
  setup) for the setup commands. `switchboard-ask` sends it too, with
  `session.ask`; `switchboard-ask "a question"` in a shell the app
  launched marks that shell's card as waiting on you, and
  `switchboard-ask --clear` takes the mark off. A Claude Code session
  may add `--confirm`, `--choice "<option>"` (once per option) or
  `--text`; the owner answers on the card, and the answer comes back
  as the session's next prompt, `Owner answered "<question>": <answer>`,
  once its turn has ended.
- `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET=<name>`: use another tmux socket name.
- `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT=<port>`: bind the remote port there instead
  of the port in `identity.json`, so two instances can run on one
  machine; `0` picks a free one. The port answers `/api/v1/info` to
  anyone and every other read to a paired device; pair one from the
  settings menu's Remote devices dialog, and read with the token it
  was given (`curl --insecure` trusts any certificate; a real client
  pins the key hash the dialog shows):
  `curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://127.0.0.1:43187/api/v1/waiting`.
  The Swift client's command-line browser does the pinned version:
  `client/README.md`; the dialog's "Copy invite" puts the QR code's
  text on the clipboard, so `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`
  pairs it. Script lines `remote-listen lan <port>` and
  `pairing <code>` put an instance on the network with a window open.
- `DISPATCH_DATA_DIR=<dir>`: where the Dispatch page looks for
  `dispatch.sock` and where its console opens (the `dispatch` binary
  reads the same variable). Tickets' trees go under
  `~/.dispatch/worktrees` regardless, or wherever `dispatch worktrees
  <path>` (also on the Dispatch page) points; the setting is
  `<dir>/settings.json`. `<dir>/events.jsonl` is the event log
  `dispatch events` and `wait` read, and `<dir>/runner.json` the
  runner's status after its last pass, which `dispatch health` reads.
  `<dir>/lock` is the writer lock, with a line naming its holder, and
  `<dir>/tickets/<id>/closing.lock` is held by whichever `dispatch` is
  finishing that ticket's close; both are lock files, not records.
----
### Layout

```
src/main.rs              launcher: wires real adapters, opens the window
src/bin/switchboard-hook.rs  helper Claude Code hooks call (std only)
src/bin/switchboard-env.rs   runs one child with a session's environment sets, resolved over the control port with its launch token; the sets' setup commands (std and the wire crate only)
src/bin/switchboard-ask.rs   marks the session it runs in as asking the owner a one-line question, or a confirm, a choice or a line of text whose answer comes back as its next prompt, or clears it, over the control port with its launch token (std and the wire crate only)
src/lib.rs               module tree and the layering rules
src/core/
  model.rs               durable data model (Project, SessionRecord, ResumeHandle, CardState)
  action.rs              AppAction, Effect, Clock, AppCore::dispatch, read model for the UI
  reconcile.rs           StoreLoaded / HostListed: card states, autostart services, spawn specs
  sessions.rs            launch, idempotent return, resume preflight, Codex serialization
tests/control.rs         the control port over a real socket with fakes: ops on records, logged replies, interrupted launches, a non-replayable command logged before it runs and answered `interrupted` on a retry, a pane's screen with secrets named
tests/remote.rs          the remote port over a real TLS listener with fakes (the control scope: a read device refused by name, a send typed once per op and a repeat answered from the log, a resume launching once, trust answering the folder question once, the bad bodies; a conversation paged by turn, from `last` or `before` a held turn, a page carrying the head of a tool result and the turn alone carrying it whole, its last response at the conversation's revision, a shell refused, a watched conversation moving as the transcript grows; a command's runs, a run's output masked, a missing run refused, a watched run output moving as the log grows): /info to anyone, pairing with the host's key and code, a token that reads every view, revocation, scope, the allowlist, bounded strings, a redacted screen, a missing key remaking the identity, Bonjour following the listen preference, the events socket (`hello`, `changed` and `removed` from the diff, a rename and a trust question with no save, ten quiet passes emitting nothing, the event and the snapshot at one revision, overflow and revocation closing the socket), watched screens (`watch` answered `watching`, the poll emitting `changed` when a pane or its policy moves and nothing while it holds still, two reads of one text at one revision, the cap evicting the least recently read, `unwatch`, a closed socket and a revocation dropping their watches), stalled strangers filling only their pool, `/ops/{op}`, the fingerprint pass timed, and the client fixtures (`client/Fixtures`, rewritten with `SWITCHBOARD_WRITE_FIXTURES=1`)
tests/fixtures/          a small real Claude Code transcript for the parser tests
tests/live.rs            ignored: real claude / codex / Ghostty runs
tests/gate.rs            Milestone 1 gate: real store, tmux, hooks; agents ignored
scripts/test-times.sh    every test's time, serially, through libtest's `--report-time`; the slowest ten, each binary's total, the 5 s budget
scripts/ci-test.sh       CI's test step: the workspace, then one retry of the failed tests, warning `flaky:` for each that passes on it
scripts/bump.sh          the next version into Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, and the changelog's Unreleased section dated under it
scripts/release.sh       the signed bundle and its SHA-256 attached to a GitHub release tagged `v<version>`, with the changelog section as notes; what the app updates itself from
CHANGELOG.md             every user-visible change, under Unreleased until a bump
client/                  the Swift client (docs/remote-client.md §7): `SwitchboardProtocol` (the wire views as Codable, qualified refs, the envelope, the event frame and resource keys), `SwitchboardTransport` (HTTPS and the events WebSocket with the SPKI-pinning delegate, Bonjour browsing), `SwitchboardClientCore` (known servers, credentials, one connection actor per host that subscribes before it snapshots and reconciles events by revision, holds reference-counted screen watches that are resent after a reconnect, the unified store), `SwitchboardUI` (SwiftUI browser and server views), the `switchboard-remote` command-line browser, tests, `Fixtures/` shared with `tests/remote.rs`, and the apps: `project.yml` (xcodegen writes the git-ignored Xcode project from it), `Apps/SwitchboardVision/` (the visionOS entry, thin over `SwitchboardUI`: the main window with list, grid and focus layouts and the filters, and the card window group), `scripts/sim.sh` (build, run and screenshot on the simulator), `scripts/device.sh` (build, install and launch on a paired headset)
control/                 switchboard-control: the control port's wire contract (requests, replies, views, a session's transcript path among them; `session.resume` resumes an agent without a terminal and never launches fresh; `session.prompt` types a prompt only into a Claude Code agent between turns, else fails naming why) and a blocking client; std + serde only
dispatch-control/        dispatch-control: the wire contract of Dispatch's own port (tickets as views, a ticket's events after a cursor, decide, queue, take, resume, close, worktrees, a project's supervisor and `supervisor-fresh`, a ticket's `usage`: tokens by model and each session's time), how a bring-up reads, and a blocking client; std + serde only
dispatch/                the `dispatch` binary (docs/dispatch.md; docs/dispatch-agent-guide.md is the command-line guide for agents that take tickets; docs/dispatch-pipeline-guide.md builds a pipeline file up step by step, every TOML block in it checked by a test; docs/dispatch-pipeline-improvements.md is the open list of pipeline changes drawn from tickets run so far): a ticket scheduler that drives Switchboard over the control port and never links the app
  src/main.rs            CLI: take, run, runner, decide, decisions, status, queue, park, resume, close, restart, worktrees, supervisor; for a supervising agent, brief (with each subscription's undelivered lines), subscribe, unsubscribe, subscriptions, events (with `--follow --timeout`), wait, show, report, tail and health (usage errors, and a command the ticket's state never allows, exit 64); a supervisor session's command checked against what it may run first
446:client/                  the Swift client (docs/remote-client.md §7): `SwitchboardProtocol` (the wire views as Codable, qualified refs, the envelope, the event frame and resource keys), `SwitchboardTransport` (HTTPS and the events WebSocket with the SPKI-pinning delegate, Bonjour browsing), `SwitchboardClientCore` (known servers, credentials, one connection actor per host that subscribes before it snapshots and reconciles events by revision, holds reference-counted screen watches that are resent after a reconnect, the unified store), `SwitchboardUI` (SwiftUI browser and server views), the `switchboard-remote` command-line browser, tests, `Fixtures/` shared with `tests/remote.rs`, and the apps: `project.yml` (xcodegen writes the git-ignored Xcode project from it), `Apps/SwitchboardVision/` (the visionOS entry, thin over `SwitchboardUI`: the main window with list, grid and focus layouts and the filters, and the card window group), `scripts/sim.sh` (build, run and screenshot on the simulator), `scripts/device.sh` (build, install and launch on a paired headset)
482:spikes/                  Spike 0 evidence, and later spikes such as 13-dispatch-service (a Dispatch service as a Switchboard service session; which bind sees a dev server's port) 15-paste-buffer (a multi-line send as one tmux paste, bracketed only for a pane that asked) 16-base-pipeline (a merged pull request's merge commit and the base's run on it) 17-prompt-origin (telling a typed prompt from a task notification or a harness reminder) 18-tmux-argv (keeping spawn's environment values off every process's argv) 19-structured-ask (a card's answer reaching the pane as its next prompt) 20-stop-pending (what a Stop lists as background work and wakeups still in flight) and 21-evidence-writes (which writes reach an evidence directory without a permission prompt)

397	## 10. Delivery plan and acceptance criteria
398	
399	### Spike 22 — `spikes/22-remote-port`
400	
401	Before any host code, with measured results in its README:
402	
403	- A blocking HTTPS server over `std::net::TcpListener` with `rustls` and an `rcgen` certificate, a WebSocket upgrade with `tungstenite`, and requests handed to a stand-in "frame" thread over a bounded `mpsc`, as the control socket does. Measure request latency through the handoff at the app's frame rate while hidden.
404	- **Frame cost, measured, with targets.** The frame's share of a metadata request, a content handle lookup, a worker's version action and the read-model diff over a few hundred records, each timed per pass; the target is under 1 ms per pass for the port's whole share, and under 4 ms at the 99th percentile with 8 requests in a pass. The content work on the connection thread timed separately: the largest transcript in the user's data directory parsed and masked (its time and peak memory are the supported size for §4.3), a 768 KiB file read and masked, a Keychain read made slow (a locked keychain) and shown to stall only its connection. A stalled subscriber and 20 connections that stall after the TLS handshake, with a healthy paired client and the frame loop measured through both. The README records the numbers and the thresholds, and a pass that misses the target is a design finding, not a tuning note.
405	- **Content versions.** The signals of §4.4 against the cases that defeat weaker ones: a same-size in-place rewrite of a pinned file with mtime restored by `touch -r`, a replace-by-rename, a run log truncated and regrown to the same length, a transcript appended within one poll interval; each must move the version. The two-second `stat` poll over 128 keys timed.
406	- Bonjour advertisement from the Rust process on macOS, visible to a visionOS simulator; the crate or system path that works.
407	- `URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` on visionOS accepting the self-signed certificate through a pinning delegate that checks the SPKI hash and nothing weaker; the same delegate refusing a substituted certificate.
408	- The `openat` walk of §4.3 through `rustix` or `cap-std`: a pinned FIFO with no writer refused at once on its connection thread while the frame loop and a second connection keep going; a parent directory swapped for a symlink mid-walk refused.
409	- Two instances on one machine (`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR`, `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET=switchboard-test-*`, different ports) each advertising with its own key.
410	
411	Loopback-only and no auth are fine here and nowhere else.
412	
413	**Results (2026-10-12, `spikes/22-remote-port/README.md`).** The host
414	half ran: the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass against the 1 ms
415	target; a request's latency is one frame interval, since a client that
416	sends on the reply synchronizes with the frame; the pools, the 5 s
417	handshake timeout and the subscriber overflow behave as §4.1 says under
418	20 stalled connections and an unread socket, with a paired client
419	unaffected; a wrong pin fails at the handshake; `mdns-sd` advertises
420	and `dns-sd` sees it; the 146 MB largest transcript parses in 290 ms at
421	575 MB peak, which is why content work is off the frame; ctime and
422	inode catch the same-size rewrite, the rename and the regrown log. Two
423	amendments follow: content reads go to **one worker thread** with a
424	queue rather than each connection thread, so one large parse is in
425	memory at a time (§4.1 is read with that change), and the Bonjour
426	instance name carries a short id suffix beside the display name. Not
427	run: the visionOS pinning delegate and the read-model diff timing.
428	
429	### Milestone A — Host port and multi-host client foundation
430	
431	Five commits, each leaving the app running and each with its README and design.md status update. The first user-visible result is a two-host read-only client at A2; nothing waits for the synchronization machinery.
432	
433	**A0 — The conversation cache in the app.** `UiState.conversations` moves to `SwitchboardApp` as the first content cache, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version; the session, card and workflow views read it through a reference. No port code. Acceptance: the UI tests pass unchanged and the app behaves identically.
434	
435	**A1 — Identity and an authenticated read-only host.** `identity.json` (id, certificate, `server_name` and the listen preference: off the LAN by default, loopback until enabled), the key in the Keychain under its installation's account, `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`. `ports::remote`, `adapters/remote.rs` with the bounds of §4.1 and the two-step content handoff, a fake, the `Effect` and `AppAction` arms, the allowlist, the redaction function. The pairing window and QR code in the settings menu, the paired-devices dialog with scope and Revoke, `devices.json`. Endpoints: `/info`, `/pair`, projects, spaces, sets, one set, sessions, session, waiting, screen. No events yet; a reply carries `epoch` and `revision` from the counter, which only the diff of A3 will move. The screen is answered on the frame as the control port answers it (a pane snapshot, redacted); the worker handoff arrives with the screen cache of A4, since there is nothing to version before it. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status.* Tests: `tests/remote.rs` against a real socket with fakes, modelled on `tests/control.rs`, covering pairing, the pin check, scope, revocation, the allowlist and screen redaction; a UI test for the dialog. Acceptance: a paired `curl` with the pinned certificate reads every view over the LAN; an unpaired one gets `/info` and nothing else.
436	
437	**A2 — Two hosts and the first client.** Bonjour advertisement and the Linux stub. 476	- A host's IP changes; Bonjour rediscovers it under the same pinned key (client, spike).
477	- Two advertisements claim one `server_id` with different keys: no automatic trust or merge (client).
478	- A substituted certificate during first pairing: the client refuses to send the code; and a `/pair` carrying another host's `spki_sha256` is refused by the host.
479	- Three wrong codes from three concurrent connections close the one pairing window; a fourth, correct, is refused. A consumed code is refused on the next `/pair`. 480	- After Revoke, the device's next request fails and its WebSocket is closed. After a key rotation, `devices.json` is empty, every old token fails, and the dialog says the pairings are gone; the client, seeing the new key under a known `server_id`, sends nothing and asks to pair again.
481	- A scope lowered in the dialog refuses the device's next `send`; raised, allows it; no request over the port changes a scope.
482	- A mutation dispatched between a subscriber's `hello` and its first snapshot, and another during a multi-resource sync: the client ends with the host's state (host test on the ordering, client test on the reconciliation).
483	- An older snapshot reply arriving after a newer one is dropped by revision (client).
484	- The host restarts: the new `epoch` makes the client refetch everything.
485	- A `send` whose process is killed after the keys went into the pane and before the reply line (the fake host records the write, the fake log fails the reply append): the retry with the same op is answered `interrupted` and nothing is sent twice. A failed request-line append refuses the send and sends nothing. A dropped HTTP response after a logged reply is answered from the log.
486	- `unknown` for an op that never reached the frame; a resubmit runs once.
487	- The configured secret appears in a prompt, a tool result, a final response, a run's output, and a pinned non-dotenv text file: every content endpoint returns it masked. A secret store that fails makes every content endpoint refuse rather than answer.
488	- The configured secret straddles each cut: the parser's `DETAIL_CAP` inside a tool result, the 256 KiB turn cut, the first byte of a run-output tail window, and the front cut of a last response: each reply masks it whole or drops it whole, never a fragment.
489	- A project with three hundred sessions, each with 64 KiB notes and a 100 KiB `name`, listed whole: one reply under the cap, notes cut at 4 KiB and names at 4 KiB with each field in `truncated`, no member lost; the same session read alone carries its notes whole. A session entering and leaving `waiting` emits `changed {waiting}` and the refetched collection lacks or holds it accordingly; a member missing from a whole reply at a later revision is dropped by the client, a member missing from an older reply arriving late is not.
490	- A 700 KiB file of quotation marks is under the source limit and answers `too_large` from the serialized check; a pane with 200 lines of 4 KiB each is cut by bytes after masking and marked. 491	- Content versions (F2): a pinned file rewritten in place at the same size with its mtime restored, a file replaced by rename, a run log truncated and regrown to its old length, and a transcript appended twice within one poll interval: each read after the change carries new content and a new revision, and no two different bodies for one key share a revision within an epoch. Two reads of an unchanged file carry the same revision.
492	- Frame cost (F4): a 20 MiB transcript, a 768 KiB file and a Keychain read made to block for two seconds, each requested while a second connection reads session metadata: the metadata reply arrives within a pass and the frame's time per pass stays under its budget; only the requesting connection waits. A content handle read on the frame for a record removed before the worker finishes: the worker's version action is a no-op and the reply names the handle it read.
493	- A window on the last response alone, and one on the conversation, each refresh when the transcript grows with no session metadata change; a handle rebind refreshes both.
494	- With every content cache populated, a new environment-set grant, a changed secret value, and a secret store that starts failing: unchanged screen, file and run-output sources are not served from their old masked bytes; the first two emit `changed` for the watched keys and serve newly masked text, the third refuses.
495	- A watched session's transcript grows and a watched pinned file is edited while the host shows an unrelated project, a document, the Dispatch page, and while the window is hidden: `changed` arrives within the poll interval.
496	- A space rename, a session moved between projects, a project and a session removed, a time-based rule set losing a member: the right `changed` and `removed` events, no reconnect.
497	- A set renamed and a pin moved (saved through `SaveViews`), a Claude Code pane reaching its trust question (`PromptSeen`, no save), and a Codex pane passing its quiet interval (`HostListed`, no save, no screen change): each emits `changed` for the right resource within the pass. 498	- Two reads of a watched file, a transcript and a pane separated by an external edit with no poll between them, delivered to the client in reverse order: the client ends on the newer content. A read of a session's metadata between them does not invalidate the conversation page.
499	- Closing one of two windows on a session sends no `unwatch`; closing the second does. 500	- Forget server on the client removes its token, pin, memory and views; a revocation seen on a connection drops the token and memory and keeps the views marked; nothing from a host is found on the client's disk after a relaunch (client).
501	- The subscriber queue overflows: `resync_required`, the socket closes, the host's frame loop and a second subscriber are unaffected (spike and adapter test).
502	- 20 stalled unauthenticated connections: the port stays answerable to a paired client (spike).
503	- `read_pinned`: a pin with `..`, an absolute path, an empty component; a symlink as a parent component (inside or outside the root, both refused) and as the leaf; a parent directory swapped for a symlink between two hops of the walk, driven from a second thread; a file that grows past the limit during the read; a FIFO with no writer, asserting the refusal returns at once and an unrelated request completes meanwhile; a directory and a device as the leaf. 504	- A long transcript pages by turn; one enormous turn is cut and marked; a conversation whose handle changed answers with the new `resume_id` and the client refetches from 1 (client).

509	- A restart and a rebuild under the stable signing identity keep the key readable; two data directories under one macOS account keep separate keys; a missing key makes a fresh identity and the dialog says the pairings are gone.

512	## 12. Answers to the first draft's questions
513	
514	1. **Models and ids.** `src/core/model.rs`: `SessionRecord` (`RecordId`), `Project` (`ProjectId`), `WorkingSet` (`SetId`) with `PinnedItem { target: PinTarget, rect: GridRect }`, `CardState`, `Run` (a command's or service's run with its scrollback log name). Conversations are `ports::transcript::Conversation` with `Turn { n, user, activity, final_text, .. }`, read by `adapters/transcript.rs` from Claude Code's JSONL.
515	2. **Control port reuse.** Yes, directly: `app.rs::serve` takes a `wire::Request` and returns a `wire::Reply`; `core/control.rs` maps bodies to `ControlAction`. The remote adapter is another producer of requests for the same path, with auth, the allowlist and redaction in front, and the log-before-run step added to `serve` for non-replayable commands.
516	3. **Runtime.** None to own; the frame thread is the executor and `listen`/`serve_pending` are the startup and polling hooks. Shutdown drops the listener as the control socket does.
517	4. **Events.** No bus, and no effect that reliably marks a visible change: `Save`, `SaveViews` and `SaveSettings` are three effects, and `PromptSeen` and the quiet interval in `reconcile.rs` change a card with none of them. So the port diffs the exported read models after every pass, with the clock-derived `quiet_secs` held out of the hash, and versions content where it is read (§4.4). Retained replay is not needed: a subscriber is registered on the frame thread, so subscribe-then-snapshot has no gap.
518	5. **Pinned file access.** The document preview (`ui::document::Preview::load`) is a UI loader: a metadata check and then an unbounded read, which is fine for the user's own click and not for a remote reader. The port gets `read_pinned` in the files adapter: a descriptor-anchored `openat` walk with no symlink followed and a nonblocking open, as §4.3 says, run on the connection thread.
519	6. **Per-session UI state and polling.** `UiState` (drafts, scroll, folds) is transient and never read by the core; none of it crosses to the client. The conversation cache in `UiState` and the caption poll in `refresh_captions` both follow the local view: a session not on the Mac's screen is not polled, and a document, workflow, Dispatch or ticket view polls nothing. The app also parses a transcript synchronously on the frame (`refresh_conversation`), which one frame absorbs for one session on screen and would not for every watched session. The port therefore needs its own watch set, the cache lifted to the app, and content work on the connection and worker threads, which are the app-level changes the implementation constraint allows.
520	7. **Two installations.** `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` on a `switchboard-test-*` socket; only the lock holder listens; `tests/control.rs` and `tests/gate.rs` show the pattern.
521	
522	**Implementation constraint:** no change to the egui frontend beyond A0's cache move, and no change to how the transcript parser reads or shapes a conversation. The host work is one adapter, additive wire views, a `read_pinned` method on the files port, an additive `read_masked` on the transcript reader (the mask runs inside the existing parse, before its detail cap) and an overlap read in `scrollback`, the content caches, read-model diff, two-step content handoff and watch worker in `app.rs`, the log-before-run step in `serve`, a Settings field or two, and one dialog. Anything larger is proposed separately.
523	
524	## 13. Explicit design decisions
525	
526	| Decision | v1 choice |
527	|---|---|
528	| Topology | Independent hosts, no coordinator |
529	| Multi-host | Concurrent connections and unified browsing |
530	| Resources | Sessions, projects, working sets with pins, pinned files, runs; no card resource |
531	| Identity | `identity.json` UUID and certificate; key in the Keychain per installation; clients pin the public key |
532	| Discovery | Bonjour and manual endpoints |
533	| Host runtime | Frame-thread dispatch for core state; content work on connection and worker threads; blocking std server with bounded queues; no Tokio |
534	| Contract | The `switchboard-control` wire views, extended additively, behind an allowlist |
535	| Data fetch | HTTPS JSON, every reply stamped with epoch and revision |
536	| Live changes | One WSS per host; read-model diff after every pass, content versions assigned on read, watch worker; `changed`/`removed` events; refetch |
537	| Synchronization | Subscribe, then snapshot, then reconcile by revision; full refetch on a new epoch |
538	| Idempotency | The control port's operation id and `operations.log`, non-replayable commands logged before they run |
539	| Redaction | One policy over every text leaving the port, run on whole source text before any cut; fail closed |
540	| Caps | Collections answered whole with every string bounded; only the conversation pages; scalar content cut after masking or refused whole; the limit enforced on serialized bytes |
541	| Content versions | Transcript: size and mtime (append-only); file and run log: inode, ctime and size; screen: hash; no two bodies share a revision for one key |
542	| Masked caches | Versioned by source and by the project's redaction policy fingerprint; a resolution failure refuses, never serves a cached success |
543	| Watch set | Global cap of 128, least recently read evicted, never refused; a read always versions correctly |
544	| File reads | Descriptor-anchored `openat` walk, no symlink followed, nonblocking open, 768 KiB, on the connection thread |
545	| Authentication | Pairing window with QR, key verified before the code is sent, 40-bit single-use code with one global attempt counter, 256-bit bearer token without expiry, scope set in the host dialog; Keychain on both ends; key rotation clears every pairing |
546	| Client storage | Server list and presentation state on disk, token and pin in the Keychain, every host body in memory only |
547	| Milestone A | Five commits: cache move, authenticated read-only host, two-host client, synchronization, watched content |
548	| Session execution | Always on the owning host |
549	| Resume | User-initiated only, confirmed on the client |
550	| Presentation state | Client-owned |
551	| visionOS layout | Native movable windows |
552	| Remote internet access | Deferred; protocol-compatible |
553	| iPadOS | Shared Swift core and views |

## 10. Delivery plan and acceptance criteria

### Spike 22 — `spikes/22-remote-port`

Before any host code, with measured results in its README:

- A blocking HTTPS server over `std::net::TcpListener` with `rustls` and an `rcgen` certificate, a WebSocket upgrade with `tungstenite`, and requests handed to a stand-in "frame" thread over a bounded `mpsc`, as the control socket does. Measure request latency through the handoff at the app's frame rate while hidden.
- **Frame cost, measured, with targets.** The frame's share of a metadata request, a content handle lookup, a worker's version action and the read-model diff over a few hundred records, each timed per pass; the target is under 1 ms per pass for the port's whole share, and under 4 ms at the 99th percentile with 8 requests in a pass. The content work on the connection thread timed separately: the largest transcript in the user's data directory parsed and masked (its time and peak memory are the supported size for §4.3), a 768 KiB file read and masked, a Keychain read made slow (a locked keychain) and shown to stall only its connection. A stalled subscriber and 20 connections that stall after the TLS handshake, with a healthy paired client and the frame loop measured through both. The README records the numbers and the thresholds, and a pass that misses the target is a design finding, not a tuning note.
- **Content versions.** The signals of §4.4 against the cases that defeat weaker ones: a same-size in-place rewrite of a pinned file with mtime restored by `touch -r`, a replace-by-rename, a run log truncated and regrown to the same length, a transcript appended within one poll interval; each must move the version. The two-second `stat` poll over 128 keys timed.
- Bonjour advertisement from the Rust process on macOS, visible to a visionOS simulator; the crate or system path that works.
- `URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` on visionOS accepting the self-signed certificate through a pinning delegate that checks the SPKI hash and nothing weaker; the same delegate refusing a substituted certificate.
- The `openat` walk of §4.3 through `rustix` or `cap-std`: a pinned FIFO with no writer refused at once on its connection thread while the frame loop and a second connection keep going; a parent directory swapped for a symlink mid-walk refused.
- Two instances on one machine (`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR`, `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET=switchboard-test-*`, different ports) each advertising with its own key.

Loopback-only and no auth are fine here and nowhere else.

**Results (2026-10-12, `spikes/22-remote-port/README.md`).** The host
half ran: the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass against the 1 ms
target; a request's latency is one frame interval, since a client that
sends on the reply synchronizes with the frame; the pools, the 5 s
handshake timeout and the subscriber overflow behave as §4.1 says under
20 stalled connections and an unread socket, with a paired client
unaffected; a wrong pin fails at the handshake; `mdns-sd` advertises
and `dns-sd` sees it; the 146 MB largest transcript parses in 290 ms at
575 MB peak, which is why content work is off the frame; ctime and
inode catch the same-size rewrite, the rename and the regrown log. Two
amendments follow: content reads go to **one worker thread** with a
queue rather than each connection thread, so one large parse is in
memory at a time (§4.1 is read with that change), and the Bonjour
instance name carries a short id suffix beside the display name. Not
run: the visionOS pinning delegate and the read-model diff timing.

- A mutation dispatched between a subscriber's `hello` and its first snapshot, and another during a multi-resource sync: the client ends with the host's state (host test on the ordering, client test on the reconciliation).
- An older snapshot reply arriving after a newer one is dropped by revision (client).
- The host restarts: the new `epoch` makes the client refetch everything.
- A `send` whose process is killed after the keys went into the pane and before the reply line (the fake host records the write, the fake log fails the reply append): the retry with the same op is answered `interrupted` and nothing is sent twice. A failed request-line append refuses the send and sends nothing. A dropped HTTP response after a logged reply is answered from the log.
- `unknown` for an op that never reached the frame; a resubmit runs once.
- The configured secret appears in a prompt, a tool result, a final response, a run's output, and a pinned non-dotenv text file: every content endpoint returns it masked. A secret store that fails makes every content endpoint refuse rather than answer.

- A project with three hundred sessions, each with 64 KiB notes and a 100 KiB `name`, listed whole: one reply under the cap, notes cut at 4 KiB and names at 4 KiB with each field in `truncated`, no member lost; the same session read alone carries its notes whole. A session entering and leaving `waiting` emits `changed {waiting}` and the refetched collection lacks or holds it accordingly; a member missing from a whole reply at a later revision is dropped by the client, a member missing from an older reply arriving late is not.
- A 700 KiB file of quotation marks is under the source limit and answers `too_large` from the serialized check; a pane with 200 lines of 4 KiB each is cut by bytes after masking and marked. A pinned file over the source limit answers `too_large`; a last response over the body cap is cut from the front and marked.
- Content versions (F2): a pinned file rewritten in place at the same size with its mtime restored, a file replaced by rename, a run log truncated and regrown to its old length, and a transcript appended twice within one poll interval: each read after the change carries new content and a new revision, and no two different bodies for one key share a revision within an epoch. Two reads of an unchanged file carry the same revision.
- Frame cost (F4): a 20 MiB transcript, a 768 KiB file and a Keychain read made to block for two seconds, each requested while a second connection reads session metadata: the metadata reply arrives within a pass and the frame's time per pass stays under its budget; only the requesting connection waits. A content handle read on the frame for a record removed before the worker finishes: the worker's version action is a no-op and the reply names the handle it read.
- A window on the last response alone, and one on the conversation, each refresh when the transcript grows with no session metadata change; a handle rebind refreshes both.

- A watched session's transcript grows and a watched pinned file is edited while the host shows an unrelated project, a document, the Dispatch page, and while the window is hidden: `changed` arrives within the poll interval.
