## 12. Answers to the first draft's questions

1. **Models and ids.** `src/core/model.rs`: `SessionRecord` (`RecordId`), `Project` (`ProjectId`), `WorkingSet` (`SetId`) with `PinnedItem { target: PinTarget, rect: GridRect }`, `CardState`, `Run` (a command's or service's run with its scrollback log name). Conversations are `ports::transcript::Conversation` with `Turn { n, user, activity, final_text, .. }`, read by `adapters/transcript.rs` from Claude Code's JSONL.
2. **Control port reuse.** Yes, directly: `app.rs::serve` takes a `wire::Request` and returns a `wire::Reply`; `core/control.rs` maps bodies to `ControlAction`. The remote adapter is another producer of requests for the same path, with auth, the allowlist and redaction in front, and the log-before-run step added to `serve` for non-replayable commands.
3. **Runtime.** None to own; the frame thread is the executor and `listen`/`serve_pending` are the startup and polling hooks. Shutdown drops the listener as the control socket does.
4. **Events.** No bus, and no effect that reliably marks a visible change: `Save`, `SaveViews` and `SaveSettings` are three effects, and `PromptSeen` and the quiet interval in `reconcile.rs` change a card with none of them. So the port diffs the exported read models after every pass, with the clock-derived `quiet_secs` held out of the hash, and versions content where it is read (§4.4). Retained replay is not needed: a subscriber is registered on the frame thread, so subscribe-then-snapshot has no gap.
5. **Pinned file access.** The document preview (`ui::document::Preview::load`) is a UI loader: a metadata check and then an unbounded read, which is fine for the user's own click and not for a remote reader. The port gets `read_pinned` in the files adapter: a descriptor-anchored `openat` walk with no symlink followed and a nonblocking open, as §4.3 says, run on the connection thread.
6. **Per-session UI state and polling.** `UiState` (drafts, scroll, folds) is transient and never read by the core; none of it crosses to the client. The conversation cache in `UiState` and the caption poll in `refresh_captions` both follow the local view: a session not on the Mac's screen is not polled, and a document, workflow, Dispatch or ticket view polls nothing. The app also parses a transcript synchronously on the frame (`refresh_conversation`), which one frame absorbs for one session on screen and would not for every watched session. The port therefore needs its own watch set, the cache lifted to the app, and content work on the connection and worker threads, which are the app-level changes the implementation constraint allows.
7. **Two installations.** `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` on a `switchboard-test-*` socket; only the lock holder listens; `tests/control.rs` and `tests/gate.rs` show the pattern.

**Implementation constraint:** no change to the egui frontend beyond A0's cache move, and no change to how the transcript parser reads or shapes a conversation. The host work is one adapter, additive wire views, a `read_pinned` method on the files port, an additive `read_masked` on the transcript reader (the mask runs inside the existing parse, before its detail cap) and an overlap read in `scrollback`, the content caches, read-model diff, two-step content handoff and watch worker in `app.rs`, the log-before-run step in `serve`, a Settings field or two, and one dialog. Anything larger is proposed separately.

## 13. Explicit design decisions

| Decision | v1 choice |
|---|---|
| Topology | Independent hosts, no coordinator |
| Multi-host | Concurrent connections and unified browsing |
| Resources | Sessions, projects, working sets with pins, pinned files, runs; no card resource |
| Identity | `identity.json` UUID and certificate; key in the Keychain per installation; clients pin the public key |
| Discovery | Bonjour and manual endpoints |
| Host runtime | Frame-thread dispatch for core state; content work on connection and worker threads; blocking std server with bounded queues; no Tokio |
| Contract | The `switchboard-control` wire views, extended additively, behind an allowlist |
| Data fetch | HTTPS JSON, every reply stamped with epoch and revision |
| Live changes | One WSS per host; read-model diff after every pass, content versions assigned on read, watch worker; `changed`/`removed` events; refetch |
| Synchronization | Subscribe, then snapshot, then reconcile by revision; full refetch on a new epoch |
| Idempotency | The control port's operation id and `operations.log`, non-replayable commands logged before they run |
| Redaction | One policy over every text leaving the port, run on whole source text before any cut; fail closed |
| Caps | Collections answered whole with every string bounded; only the conversation pages; scalar content cut after masking or refused whole; the limit enforced on serialized bytes |
| Content versions | Transcript: size and mtime (append-only); file and run log: inode, ctime and size; screen: hash; no two bodies share a revision for one key |
| Masked caches | Versioned by source and by the project's redaction policy fingerprint; a resolution failure refuses, never serves a cached success |
| Watch set | Global cap of 128, least recently read evicted, never refused; a read always versions correctly |
| File reads | Descriptor-anchored `openat` walk, no symlink followed, nonblocking open, 768 KiB, on the connection thread |
| Authentication | Pairing window with QR, key verified before the code is sent, 40-bit single-use code with one global attempt counter, 256-bit bearer token without expiry, scope set in the host dialog; Keychain on both ends; key rotation clears every pairing |
| Client storage | Server list and presentation state on disk, token and pin in the Keychain, every host body in memory only |
| Milestone A | Five commits: cache move, authenticated read-only host, two-host client, synchronization, watched content |
| Session execution | Always on the owning host |
| Resume | User-initiated only, confirmed on the client |
| Presentation state | Client-owned |
| visionOS layout | Native movable windows |
| Remote internet access | Deferred; protocol-compatible |
| iPadOS | Shared Swift core and views |

477	- Two advertisements claim one `server_id` with different keys: no automatic trust or merge (client).

479	- Three wrong codes from three concurrent connections close the one pairing window; a fourth, correct, is refused. A consumed code is refused on the next `/pair`. 482	- A mutation dispatched between a subscriber's `hello` and its first snapshot, and another during a multi-resource sync: the client ends with the host's state (host test on the ordering, client test on the reconciliation).
483	- An older snapshot reply arriving after a newer one is dropped by revision (client).
484	- The host restarts: the new `epoch` makes the client refetch everything.
485	- A `send` whose process is killed after the keys went into the pane and before the reply line (the fake host records the write, the fake log fails the reply append): the retry with the same op is answered `interrupted` and nothing is sent twice. 512	## 12. Answers to the first draft's questions
513	
514	1. **Models and ids.** `src/core/model.rs`: `SessionRecord` (`RecordId`), `Project` (`ProjectId`), `WorkingSet` (`SetId`) with `PinnedItem { target: PinTarget, rect: GridRect }`, `CardState`, `Run` (a command's or service's run with its scrollback log name). Conversations are `ports::transcript::Conversation` with `Turn { n, user, activity, final_text, .. }`, read by `adapters/transcript.rs` from Claude Code's JSONL.
515	2. **Control port reuse.** Yes, directly: `app.rs::serve` takes a `wire::Request` and returns a `wire::Reply`; `core/control.rs` maps bodies to `ControlAction`. The remote adapter is another producer of requests for the same path, with auth, the allowlist and redaction in front, and the log-before-run step added to `serve` for non-replayable commands.
516	3. **Runtime.** None to own; the frame thread is the executor and `listen`/`serve_pending` are the startup and polling hooks. Shutdown drops the listener as the control socket does.
517	4. **Events.** No bus, and no effect that reliably marks a visible change: `Save`, `SaveViews` and `SaveSettings` are three effects, and `PromptSeen` and the quiet interval in `reconcile.rs` change a card with none of them. So the port diffs the exported read models after every pass, with the clock-derived `quiet_secs` held out of the hash, and versions content where it is read (§4.4). Retained replay is not needed: a subscriber is registered on the frame thread, so subscribe-then-snapshot has no gap.
518	5. **Pinned file access.** The document preview (`ui::document::Preview::load`) is a UI loader: a metadata check and then an unbounded read, which is fine for the user's own click and not for a remote reader. The port gets `read_pinned` in the files adapter: a descriptor-anchored `openat` walk with no symlink followed and a nonblocking open, as §4.3 says, run on the connection thread.
519	6. **Per-session UI state and polling.** `UiState` (drafts, scroll, folds) is transient and never read by the core; none of it crosses to the client. The conversation cache in `UiState` and the caption poll in `refresh_captions` both follow the local view: a session not on the Mac's screen is not polled, and a document, workflow, Dispatch or ticket view polls nothing. The app also parses a transcript synchronously on the frame (`refresh_conversation`), which one frame absorbs for one session on screen and would not for every watched session. The port therefore needs its own watch set, the cache lifted to the app, and content work on the connection and worker threads, which are the app-level changes the implementation constraint allows.
520	7. **Two installations.** `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` on a `switchboard-test-*` socket; only the lock holder listens; `tests/control.rs` and `tests/gate.rs` show the pattern.
521	
522	**Implementation constraint:** no change to the egui frontend beyond A0's cache move, and no change to how the transcript parser reads or shapes a conversation. The host work is one adapter, additive wire views, a `read_pinned` method on the files port, an additive `read_masked` on the transcript reader (the mask runs inside the existing parse, before its detail cap) and an overlap read in `scrollback`, the content caches, read-model diff, two-step content handoff and watch worker in `app.rs`, the log-before-run step in `serve`, a Settings field or two, and one dialog. Anything larger is proposed separately.
523	
524	## 13. Explicit design decisions
525	
526	| Decision | v1 choice |
527	|---|---|
528	| Topology | Independent hosts, no coordinator |
529	| Multi-host | Concurrent connections and unified browsing |
530	| Resources | Sessions, projects, working sets with pins, pinned files, runs; no card resource |
531	| Identity | `identity.json` UUID and certificate; key in the Keychain per installation; clients pin the public key |
532	| Discovery | Bonjour and manual endpoints |
533	| Host runtime | Frame-thread dispatch for core state; content work on connection and worker threads; blocking std server with bounded queues; no Tokio |
534	| Contract | The `switchboard-control` wire views, extended additively, behind an allowlist |
535	| Data fetch | HTTPS JSON, every reply stamped with epoch and revision |
536	| Live changes | One WSS per host; read-model diff after every pass, content versions assigned on read, watch worker; `changed`/`removed` events; refetch |
537	| Synchronization | Subscribe, then snapshot, then reconcile by revision; full refetch on a new epoch |
538	| Idempotency | The control port's operation id and `operations.log`, non-replayable commands logged before they run |
539	| Redaction | One policy over every text leaving the port, run on whole source text before any cut; fail closed |
540	| Caps | Collections answered whole with every string bounded; only the conversation pages; scalar content cut after masking or refused whole; the limit enforced on serialized bytes |
541	| Content versions | Transcript: size and mtime (append-only); file and run log: inode, ctime and size; screen: hash; no two bodies share a revision for one key |
542	| Masked caches | Versioned by source and by the project's redaction policy fingerprint; a resolution failure refuses, never serves a cached success |
543	| Watch set | Global cap of 128, least recently read evicted, never refused; a read always versions correctly |
544	| File reads | Descriptor-anchored `openat` walk, no symlink followed, nonblocking open, 768 KiB, on the connection thread |
545	| Authentication | Pairing window with QR, key verified before the code is sent, 40-bit single-use code with one global attempt counter, 256-bit bearer token without expiry, scope set in the host dialog; Keychain on both ends; key rotation clears every pairing |
546	| Client storage | Server list and presentation state on disk, token and pin in the Keychain, every host body in memory only |
547	| Milestone A | Five commits: cache move, authenticated read-only host, two-host client, synchronization, watched content |
548	| Session execution | Always on the owning host |
549	| Resume | User-initiated only, confirmed on the client |
550	| Presentation state | Client-owned |
551	| visionOS layout | Native movable windows |
552	| Remote internet access | Deferred; protocol-compatible |
553	| iPadOS | Shared Swift core and views |

The latency is one pass interval, not half: a client that sends on the
reply synchronizes with the frame. The interval is longer than the
sleep (22 ms for a 16 ms sleep, 108 for 100) because `thread::sleep`
overshoots by 6 to 8 ms on this Mac; eframe paces its own loop, so the
app will not. `TCP_NODELAY` and a one-record reply changed nothing,
which is how the overshoot was found. **The frame's share is under
0.25 ms per pass at the worst, against the 1 ms target.** A fresh TLS
handshake costs nothing visible beside the frame interval.

**Overflow.** A subscriber that stops reading while 4 KiB events flow
at the frame rate: after 12 s unread, the drain gave 391 frames

# Spike 23: a browser on the remote port

The questions the web control surface (#230) rests on that no source
settled (`facts.md` for #230, Unresolved 3 and 6): does a browser store
and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set by a
self-signed certificate with no subject alternative name on an
IP-literal host once the owner has clicked through its warning; do two
servers on one address with per-server cookie names (`__Host-sb-<id>`)
keep their cookies apart; does the page's `connect-src 'self'` admit
`wss:` to the same host; and how many of a browser's parallel
connections a page load costs against the port's pool of four.

Standalone crate, not built by the app. Builds into the repo's shared
`target/` like every crate under this tree.

## What it does

`src/main.rs` is a throwaway HTTPS server over a certificate made as
the app's `make_identity` makes it (P-256, self-signed, CN only). It
serves one page under the app's exact Content-Security-Policy whose
script asks `/set` to set `__Host-sb-<id>=tok-<id>` as an `HttpOnly`
cookie, reads `/me` back (the server echoes the `Cookie` header it
received), prints `document.cookie` (which should be empty), and opens
`wss://<host>/ws`, reporting `open`, `error` or the close code. Two
servers with different `--id` and `--port` on one address show whether
the second's cookie overwrites the first's: after both pages have
loaded, `/me` on either should list both cookies, each under its own
name.

## Commands

```sh
cd spikes/23-web-page
cargo run --release -- --port 8443 --id alpha      # one terminal
cargo run --release -- --port 8444 --id beta       # another
# On the Mac: open https://127.0.0.1:8443/ and https://127.0.0.1:8444/ in
# Safari and in Chrome, proceed past the certificate warning, read the
# <pre>. On a phone: the Mac's LAN address in place of 127.0.0.1.
```

Headless Chrome with `--ignore-certificate-errors` is a weaker check
(it bypasses the warning rather than recording an exception) and is
how the Mac half can be driven without a hand:

```sh
chrome --headless=new --ignore-certificate-errors --user-data-dir=/tmp/sb-spike23 \
  --virtual-time-budget=6000 --dump-dom https://127.0.0.1:8443/
chrome --headless=new --ignore-certificate-errors --user-data-dir=/tmp/sb-spike23 \
  --virtual-time-budget=6000 --dump-dom https://127.0.0.1:8444/
```

## Results (2026-10-24)

**Browser: not run.** The implementing session could run the servers
but not a browser, so the cookie, the two-server jar and the `wss:`
questions stand as the plan left them: acceptance steps 1 to 4 rest on
the owner's phone and on the two commands above. The host side builds
to the favourable answer (the cookie transport) and the fallback the
plan names (the token held by the page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`
echo) is the owner's call if a browser refuses the cookie.

**Parallel connections against the harness: measured.** The test
`page_loads_free_their_slot_and_have_their_own_window` in
`tests/remote.rs` opens five page requests at once against the real
listener's unauthenticated pool of four, each reply closing its
connection:

| run | served |
|---|---|
| five parallel `GET /app.js` | 4 of 5 |

The fifth is dropped at accept because the four are still inside their
TLS handshakes when it arrives; a browser retries a dropped connection,
and a page load is three requests, so a single phone never meets the
limit. Five sequential loads all succeed, which is what `Connection:
close` buys: a kept connection would hold a slot for the 30 s idle
timeout. The test asserts at least four and prints the count with
`--nocapture`.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.

- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

# Spike 23: a browser on the remote port

The questions the web control surface (#230) rests on that no source
settled (`facts.md` for #230, Unresolved 3 and 6): does a browser store
and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set by a
self-signed certificate with no subject alternative name on an
IP-literal host once the owner has clicked through its warning; do two
servers on one address with per-server cookie names (`__Host-sb-<id>`)
keep their cookies apart; does the page's `connect-src 'self'` admit
`wss:` to the same host; and how many of a browser's parallel
connections a page load costs against the port's pool of four.

Standalone crate, not built by the app. Builds into the repo's shared
`target/` like every crate under this tree.

## What it does

`src/main.rs` is a throwaway HTTPS server over a certificate made as
the app's `make_identity` makes it (P-256, self-signed, CN only). It
serves one page under the app's exact Content-Security-Policy whose
script asks `/set` to set `__Host-sb-<id>=tok-<id>` as an `HttpOnly`
cookie, reads `/me` back (the server echoes the `Cookie` header it
received), prints `document.cookie` (which should be empty), and opens
`wss://<host>/ws`, reporting `open`, `error` or the close code. Two
servers with different `--id` and `--port` on one address show whether
the second's cookie overwrites the first's: after both pages have
loaded, `/me` on either should list both cookies, each under its own
name.

## Commands

```sh
cd spikes/23-web-page
cargo run --release -- --port 8443 --id alpha      # one terminal
cargo run --release -- --port 8444 --id beta       # another
# On the Mac: open https://127.0.0.1:8443/ and https://127.0.0.1:8444/ in
# Safari and in Chrome, proceed past the certificate warning, read the
# <pre>. On a phone: the Mac's LAN address in place of 127.0.0.1.
```

Headless Chrome with `--ignore-certificate-errors` is a weaker check
(it bypasses the warning rather than recording an exception) and is
how the Mac half can be driven without a hand:

```sh
chrome --headless=new --ignore-certificate-errors --user-data-dir=/tmp/sb-spike23 \
  --virtual-time-budget=6000 --dump-dom https://127.0.0.1:8443/
chrome --headless=new --ignore-certificate-errors --user-data-dir=/tmp/sb-spike23 \
  --virtual-time-budget=6000 --dump-dom https://127.0.0.1:8444/
```

## Results (2026-10-24)

**Browser: not run.** The implementing session could run the servers
but not a browser, so the cookie, the two-server jar and the `wss:`
questions stand as the plan left them: acceptance steps 1 to 4 rest on
the owner's phone and on the two commands above. The host side builds
to the favourable answer (the cookie transport) and the fallback the
plan names (the token held by the page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`
echo) is the owner's call if a browser refuses the cookie.

**Parallel connections against the harness: measured.** The test
`page_loads_free_their_slot_and_have_their_own_window` in
`tests/remote.rs` opens five page requests at once against the real
listener's unauthenticated pool of four, each reply closing its
connection:

| run | served |
|---|---|
| five parallel `GET /app.js` | 4 of 5 |

The fifth is dropped at accept because the four are still inside their
TLS handshakes when it arrives; a browser retries a dropped connection,
and a page load is three requests, so a single phone never meets the
limit. Five sequential loads all succeed, which is what `Connection:
close` buys: a kept connection would hold a slot for the 30 s idle
timeout. The test asserts at least four and prints the count with
`--nocapture`.

# Changelog

Every user-visible change goes under Unreleased as it lands.
`scripts/bump.sh` moves that section under the next version with the
date, and `scripts/release.sh` publishes that section as the release
notes. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com)
and the versions follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.4.1] - 2026-10-21

- Dispatch takes an issue once per project rather than once across the data directory, so a second project on the same repository can take an issue the first already holds.

## [0.4.0] - 2026-10-21

### Added

- Dispatch reports each ticket's tokens by model and agent time, per attempt, stage and ticket, in `dispatch report` and a Usage tab on the ticket page.

### Fixed

- The session page's token count counts each message once, not once per content block, skips Claude Code's synthetic messages, and names each model when a session used more than one.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-10-19

### Added

- A session can be opened from the headset: a plus button on the Sessions tab, or "New session in this project" on a listed session, opens a Claude Code, Codex or shell session in a project on any connected host paired under the control scope, in the project's root or a directory under it, with a first message for an agent; the new session's window opens on the reply. The remote port takes `POST projects/{id}/sessions` for it and lists `create` among its capabilities.
- The remote port serves Dispatch's tickets: a listing with each ticket's standing and decisions, one ticket with its body, attempts and lanes, and under the control scope a decision answered or a parked ticket resumed. The headset gets a Tickets tab on it.
- The headset reads what each stage produced: every attempt lists its notes and other artifacts, its checks log, its review rounds' findings and responses and its evidence, each opened with a tap as text or as a picture; a ticket's timeline is read from the runner's event log; and a closable ticket can be closed. The ticket list is ordered last moved first, with a menu for the order (waiting first, newest, by project), the hosts, projects and states (closed hidden unless asked) and a "waiting on me" switch.

### Changed

- The headset's conversation view follows the end as a mode: it is held at the end, nothing growing under it can leave it behind, and a button at the right edge releases it for reading; the ellipsis at the foot returns it to following. Before, a new turn that began with a tool call could push the end off screen and switch following off, and the view could jump up to the turn it last held at the top.

### Fixed

- The headset's filter menu no longer jumps back to its top every couple of seconds while open: it is rebuilt only when a host or a session state it lists changes, not on every refresh.

## [0.2.1] - 2026-10-15

### Fixed

- A first launch on a display macOS reports at an odd scale (a Sidecar
  screen) no longer aborts before the window shows: the GPU's own
  texture limit is asked for instead of egui's 8192 (#185).

## [0.2.0] - 2026-10-15

### Added

- The app's version in the Settings menu, with a check for a newer
  release on GitHub twenty seconds after launch and hourly after that.
  A newer one is offered for download, checked against its published
  checksum and the running app's signing team, and installed on
  "Restart to update", which quits, swaps the bundle in place and
  relaunches.
- The headset pairs with a discovered host by its typed code, with the
  host's key shown for a check by eye, since visionOS gives an app no
  camera.
- `scripts/bump.sh` and `scripts/release.sh`: the version, this
  changelog and a GitHub release with the signed bundle and its
  checksum.
- The host's `/info` reply names the app's version, and the headset
  shows it beside each known host.

## [0.1.0] - 2026-10-14

### Added

- The remote port and the visionOS client: pairing with a pinned key,
  sessions and working sets from several hosts, live screens,
  conversations, run output, the draft and dictation into the host's
  editor, commands under the control scope.
- The first GitHub release, built by hand.

lines: - **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.

- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:

-  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
-  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;

+  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's. A request for one of the web page's files (`GET /`, `/app.js`, `/app.css`) is an unauthenticated connection like any other: it counts in the pool from accept, is answered on the connection thread from the embedded bytes without reaching the frame, and its reply carries `Connection: close`, so a load frees its slot at once rather than holding it for the idle timeout (Spike 23 measured four of five parallel page requests served against the pool);

+  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener, `/info` sixty, and the page's files 120 (`Limits.page`; a load is three); past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
- a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
- one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);

- the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;

lines: New read models, added to the wire crate:

- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).

-- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.

+- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it, and is not on the port at all yet: the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs`), the record stores no excerpt, and `SessionView` has no field for it. Putting it on the wire means moving that function into the core and adding an additive `SessionView` field; until then a device's row shows the name, kind, card word, `waiting_reason` and the time since `last_activity_ms`.

- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.

- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
- the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);

So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. - **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, or, for a browser, as the cookie below; never in a URL.
- **A browser's token is a cookie.** `/pair` with `transport: "cookie"` answers `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` and a body with no `token`, so the page's script never holds it. The host accepts that cookie, matched by exact name in the `Cookie` header with every other cookie ignored, as a credential beside the bearer header; the bearer wins when both are present. The name carries the server id because cookies ignore ports: two instances on one Mac share the page's cookie jar, and a fixed name would have the second pairing overwrite the first's token. A request authenticated by the cookie alone that is not a plain `GET` (a `POST`, or the upgrade to `/events`) must carry `Origin: https://<Host header>` or is refused 403 `origin`; a bearer request is exempt. The weaker trust is the browser's: it cannot pin the key, the certificate warning's click-through is its trust step, a relay that terminates TLS defeats the page's key comparison, and another HTTPS service on the same address receives the cookie too (`__Host-` fixes the host and path, not the port). The dialog says so and says to pair a browser only on a network you trust. The host cannot say "revoked" (a revoked token and an unknown one are one 401); the page reads `/info` and tells "removed on the host" (same `server_id` and key) from "identity changed".

- Milestone A is five commits, A0 to A4, with a two-host read-only client at
  A2 (F1).

A web control surface (2026-10-24, #230) rides on the same port: three
embedded files served before pairing, a pairing from the invite URL's
fragment, the token as a per-server `HttpOnly` cookie beside the bearer
header, `GET /me`, and an `Origin` rule for cookie-authenticated writes.
§4.1, §4.3 and §5 carry the details.

## 1. Product goals

input.new_string:
- at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's. A request for one of the web page's files (`GET /`, `/app.js`, `/app.css`) is an unauthenticated connection like any other: it counts in the pool from accept, is answered on the connection thread from the embedded bytes without reaching the frame, and its reply carries `Connection: close`, so a load frees its slot at once rather than holding it for the idle timeout (Spike 23 measured four of five parallel page requests served against the pool);
  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener, `/info` sixty, and the page's files 120 (`Limits.page`; a load is three); past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;

input.new_string:
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, or, for a browser, as the cookie below; never in a URL.
- **A browser's token is a cookie.** `/pair` with `transport: "cookie"` answers `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` and a body with no `token`, so the page's script never holds it. The host accepts that cookie, matched by exact name in the `Cookie` header with every other cookie ignored, as a credential beside the bearer header; the bearer wins when both are present. The name carries the server id because cookies ignore ports: two instances on one Mac share the page's cookie jar, and a fixed name would have the second pairing overwrite the first's token. A request authenticated by the cookie alone that is not a plain `GET` (a `POST`, or the upgrade to `/events`) must carry `Origin: https://<Host header>` or is refused 403 `origin`; a bearer request is exempt. The weaker trust is the browser's: it cannot pin the key, the certificate warning's click-through is its trust step, a relay that terminates TLS defeats the page's key comparison, and another HTTPS service on the same address receives the cookie too (`__Host-` fixes the host and path, not the port). The dialog says so and says to pair a browser only on a network you trust. The host cannot say "revoked" (a revoked token and an unknown one are one 401); the page reads `/info` and tells "removed on the host" (same `server_id` and key) from "identity changed".

input.new_string:
unsigned host freezes on the Keychain prompt while a device asks for
  a draft; the signed bundle never prompts. Remote access off the LAN
  is §9 of the spec, deferred.
- **A web page on the port (2026-10-24, #230).** The port serves three
  embedded files (`web/index.html`, `app.js`, `app.css`, the table in
  `src/adapters/web.rs`) before pairing, answered on the connection
  thread with `Connection: close` so a load never waits on the frame
  and never holds one of the four unauthenticated slots, under a
  Content-Security-Policy that admits nothing but the page's own files
  and API, and in a window of 120 a minute. The pairing invite is now
  the page's URL with the code, key hash and server id in the fragment
  (`core::remote::invite_url`), which no request carries, so a
  phone's camera opens the page and the page compares the key and id
  with `/info` before it sends the code; the Swift client parses the
  URL and the older JSON alike. A browser's token is a cookie the host
  sets, `__Host-sb-<server_id>` with `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and
  `SameSite=Strict`, named for the server so two instances on one Mac
  keep their cookies apart; the host accepts it beside the bearer
  header, and a cookie-authenticated write or upgrade must carry the
  page's own `Origin` (403 `origin` otherwise). `GET /me` tells the
  page its scope. The page lists projects with a waiting session first
  and waiting sessions first within one, shows a Claude Code session's
  last response or any other's screen, sends a reply under `control`
  with a kept op so a retry never types twice, polls `/waiting` every
  3 s and refetches on a moved revision, and uses the events socket
  when a browser connects it (Safari may not, over a click-through
  certificate). A 401 is read off `/info`: same id and key means
  "removed on the host", else "identity changed". The dialog shows
  the QR from the URL, says "This Mac only" in place of the address
  while the port is loopback, and says what a browser's trust is: no
  pin, the certificate warning's click-through, a network you trust.
  Spike 23 could not drive a browser in the implementing session, so
  whether Safari and Chrome keep the cookie over a click-through
  certificate on an IP host, and whether `wss:` connects, rest on the
  owner's phone; the fallback the plan names is the token held by the
  page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo. Known gaps: the card's
  one-line excerpt is not on the wire (a `SessionView` field to add);
  a trusted-certificate path (an IP SAN, a downloadable certificate or
  a local CA) is its own issue; the Swift client does not yet read
  `/me`.

## Versioning and updates (2026-10-15)

input.new_string:
unsigned host freezes on the Keychain prompt while a device asks for
  a draft; the signed bundle never prompts. Remote access off the LAN
  is §9 of the spec, deferred.
- **A web page on the port (2026-10-24, #230).** The port serves three
  embedded files (`web/index.html`, `app.js`, `app.css`, the table in
  `src/adapters/web.rs`) before pairing, answered on the connection
  thread with `Connection: close` so a load never waits on the frame
  and never holds one of the four unauthenticated slots, under a
  Content-Security-Policy that admits nothing but the page's own files
  and API, and in a window of 120 a minute. The pairing invite is now
  the page's URL with the code, key hash and server id in the fragment
  (`core::remote::invite_url`), which no request carries, so a
  phone's camera opens the page and the page compares the key and id
  with `/info` before it sends the code; the Swift client parses the
  URL and the older JSON alike. A browser's token is a cookie the host
  sets, `__Host-sb-<server_id>` with `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and
  `SameSite=Strict`, named for the server so two instances on one Mac
  keep their cookies apart; the host accepts it beside the bearer
  header, and a cookie-authenticated write or upgrade must carry the
  page's own `Origin` (403 `origin` otherwise). `GET /me` tells the
  page its scope. The page lists projects with a waiting session first
  and waiting sessions first within one, shows a Claude Code session's
  last response or any other's screen, sends a reply under `control`
  with a kept op so a retry never types twice, polls `/waiting` every
  3 s and refetches on a moved revision, and uses the events socket
  when a browser connects it (Safari may not, over a click-through
  certificate). A 401 is read off `/info`: same id and key means
  "removed on the host", else "identity changed". The dialog shows
  the QR from the URL, says "This Mac only" in place of the address
  while the port is loopback, and says what a browser's trust is: no
  pin, the certificate warning's click-through, a network you trust.
  Spike 23 could not drive a browser in the implementing session, so
  whether Safari and Chrome keep the cookie over a click-through
  certificate on an IP host, and whether `wss:` connects, rest on the
  owner's phone; the fallback the plan names is the token held by the
  page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo. Known gaps: the card's
  one-line excerpt is not on the wire (a `SessionView` field to add);
  a trusted-certificate path (an IP SAN, a downloadable certificate or
  a local CA) is its own issue; the Swift client does not yet read
  `/me`.

Serve a web control surface from the remote port, paired from a URL whose fragment carries the code

The host serves three embedded files (web/index.html, app.js, app.css)
from the port it already has, before pairing, on the connection thread
with Connection: close, under a Content-Security-Policy that admits only
the page's own files and API, in a window of 120 a minute. The pairing
invite is now the page's URL with the code, key hash and server id in
the fragment, which no request carries; the page compares them with
/info before it sends the code. A browser's token is an HttpOnly cookie
named for the server, accepted beside the bearer header; a cookie
write or upgrade must carry the page's own Origin. The page lists the
sessions with the waiting ones first, shows a Claude Code session's
last response or any other's screen, sends a reply under control with
a kept op, polls /waiting and uses the events socket when a browser
connects it, and reads a 401 off /info as "removed" or "identity
changed".

Spike 23 could not drive a browser in the implementing session; the
cookie, two-server and wss: questions rest on the owner's phone, and
the harness measured four of five parallel page requests served
against the pool of four.

Contract additions:
- No new AppAction or Effect variant, no port method.
- RemoteReply.headers, RemoteReply::new; RemoteRequest.{cookie, origin, host}.
- core::remote::invite_url.
- Wire: GET /api/v1/me; /pair request field transport; the
  __Host-sb-<server_id> cookie accepted as a credential beside the
  bearer header; the 403 code origin; GET /, /app.js, /app.css before
  pairing; the invite text is a URL (the JSON still parses in the Swift
  client).
- No change to model.rs, control/, or any schema version.
EOF
git status --short && git log --oneline -1

# Implement notes: sb-230 web control surface (v5rev-fable-leanb2)

Branch `stage/sb-230-implement-v5rev-fable-leanb2`, one commit as the plan
asked, on top of `7fe8949` (Release 0.4.1). Not pushed, no pull request.
`git status` is clean after the commit.

## The commit

`fd5295b` "Serve a web control surface from the remote port, paired from
a URL whose fragment carries the code", with the plan's contract-additions
list in the body. 24 files, +3104/-160.

Before committing: `cargo fmt --all`, `cargo clippy --locked --workspace
--all-targets -- -D warnings` (clean), `cargo test --locked --workspace`
(every binary green; `tests/remote.rs` 52 passed including the eight new
tests, `tests/ui.rs` 205, core 535). `swift test --filter
SwitchboardProtocolTests` in `client/` passes (4 tests). The Linux
cross-clippy for `dispatch` was not run: no `cfg(target_os)` arm and
nothing platform-only was touched.

## What was built, by the plan's order of work

1. **Spike 23** `spikes/23-web-page/`: a standalone crate (a throwaway
   HTTPS server over a P-256 CN-only certificate as `make_identity` makes
   it, a page under the app's exact CSP that sets `__Host-sb-<id>`
   HttpOnly, reads it back, prints `document.cookie`, and opens `wss:`),
   plus a README with the commands. **The browser half is "not run"**: the
   session could build and start the two servers but every browser launch
   and direct binary run needed an approval the non-interactive session
   cannot grant. The parallel-connection measurement was done against the
   harness instead and recorded: 4 of 5 parallel page requests served
   against the pool of 4; five sequential loads all succeed.
2. `RemoteReply::new`, `RemoteReply.headers`, `RemoteRequest.{cookie,
   origin, host}`; `respond` writes the reply's headers plus
   `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on
   every JSON reply. `remote::cookie_value` reads a cookie by exact name.
3. `authenticate` takes the bearer, else this host's cookie
   (`__Host-sb-<server_id>`), and refuses a cookie-only non-GET or
   upgrade without `Origin: https://<Host>` as 403 `origin`. `/pair`
   takes `transport: "cookie"`: `Set-Cookie` with `Max-Age=34560000;
   Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, no `token` in the body.
   `GET /api/v1/me` under `read`.
4. `src/adapters/web.rs` (the table of three files, `CSP`, `HEADERS`,
   `page()`); page paths answered in `connection` before the frame with
   `Connection: close`; `Limits.page` at 120/minute (`PAGE_PER_MINUTE`).
5. `core::remote::invite_url` (re-exported from `core`); the dialog
   builds the QR and "Copy invite" from it, shows `MAC_ONLY_NOTICE` in
   place of the address while `listen.lan` is off, and adds the browser
   sentence beside the redaction one. Swift `PairingInvite.parse` takes
   the URL (fragment `code`, `key`, `id`; the authority as the one
   address) and the JSON.
6. `web/index.html`, `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`, `web/app.test.js`:
   boot from the fragment with `history.replaceState` first, `/info`
   comparison, pair by cookie, `/me`, the grouped list (waiting first),
   last response or screen, the reply box under `control` with a kept
   op, `/waiting` poll at 3 s with revision ordering, the events socket
   as an enhancement (20 s poll while connected, 5 s doubling to 60 s
   retry), the `/info` inference on every 401, `textContent` only. The
   routes live in one `ROUTES` table with `{id}` placeholders.
7. Docs: `remote-client.md` §0 dated paragraph, §4.1 pool and window,
   §4.3 rows for the page files, `/pair transport` and `/me`, the
   excerpt sentence corrected, §5 pre-pairing surface, the URL invite,
   the cookie paragraph, the headers; `design.md` a dated paragraph with
   known gaps at the end of "Remote client"; README Layout rows for
   `web/`, `src/adapters/web.rs`, the spike, the dialog and the test
   file, and the dev-aid sentence; CHANGELOG Unreleased.

## Tests added

- Core: `the_invite_is_a_url_whose_fragment_carries_the_code_and_the_key`.
- Adapter unit: cookie parsing; the reply and page writers' headers;
  `web::page` lookup.
- Host (`tests/remote.rs`): the three files with their headers and a
  closed connection, the JSON 404 for everything else outside the API
  (`/favicon.ico`, `POST /`, `/api`, `/index.html`, `HEAD /app.js`), a
  query not echoed; the page referencing only served paths with every
  `/api/v1/` string in `app.js` answering a paired device with something
  other than `not_found`, and the markup/script guards; pairing by cookie
  (attributes, no token in the body, the cookie alone reading `/me`,
  among other cookies, a native pairing unchanged); two hosts' cookies
  kept apart and the fixed name refused; the `Origin` rule on `send` and
  on the upgrade, a bearer exempt; `/me` following `SetDeviceScope`, a
  revoked cookie 401 against an unchanged `/info`; the rotated identity's
  `/info` assertion added to the existing missing-key test; the stalled
  strangers test extended with a page request failing at accept; page
  loads freeing their slot, five in parallel measured, the 121st page
  request 429 with `/info` and `/pair` untouched; `web/app.test.js`
  under `node --test` through a Rust test that skips when node is
  absent (node ran here and passed).
- UI: the "Copy invite" assertions rewritten for the URL and the
  Mac-only notice.
- Swift: the URL parses to the same invite as the JSON; a URL without
  `code` or without a fragment is an error; a trailing newline and an
  IPv6 address.

## What the plan got wrong or did not foresee

- **Reply literal count.** The plan (and facts) said about twenty
  `RemoteReply { .. }` literals in `app.rs`; there were nine (the grep
  counted function signatures returning `RemoteReply`). Converted all
  nine plus the one in `connection`.
- **`serve_remote` length.** Adding the `/me` arm pushed the function
  over clippy's 100-line limit; the catch-all refusal's message moved to
  a `NOT_ON_PORT` constant so the arm fits on one line. No behaviour
  change.
- **`subscribe_at` extension.** The plan said `subscribe_at` (`:1960`)
  "takes extra headers". It took a token; I added `subscribe_with(port,
  headers, path) -> Result<Subscriber, String>` beneath it and made
  `subscribe_at` a wrapper, since a refused upgrade needs to come back as
  an `Err` rather than a panic.
- **Swift IPv6 host.** This Foundation keeps the brackets in
  `URLComponents.host` for an IPv6 literal; the parser strips them before
  rebuilding `[host]:port`. The plan did not mention IPv6; `invite_url`
  brackets an IPv6 address as a URL needs.
- **The spike's browser half.** The plan allowed "not run" and that is
  what happened; Unresolved 1, 2 and 3 stand for the owner's phone and
  for the two Chrome commands in the spike README. The fallback (token in
  the page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo) was not built, as the
  plan said not to.
- **Pre-commit hook.** Whether `core.hooksPath` is set in this worktree
  could not be read (the config query needed approval); the four
  commands were run by hand before the commit instead.
- **Nothing scoped down.** Every item in the plan's order of work and
  test list is in the commit. The one-line excerpt on the wire, the
  trusted-certificate path and the Swift client reading `/me` are the
  plan's own follow-ups, left as listed under design.md's known gaps.
